nameStory: Tansy gets its name from the Greek word 'athanatos,' meaning immortal, because its flowers last so long and the plant was once thought to grant immortality. The 'golden buttons' nickname comes from its bright yellow flower clusters that look exactly like tiny round buttons sewn onto green fabric. Early settlers called it 'bitter buttons' after tasting its intensely bitter leaves.
description: Tansy is a sturdy perennial herb that grows 2-4 feet tall with deeply divided, fern-like leaves and clusters of bright yellow button-shaped flowers. Originally from Europe, this hardy plant has naturalized throughout New England and can form large colonies. The entire plant has a strong, camphor-like scent that's unmistakable once you've smelled it. Its upright stems are topped with flat clusters of golden flowers that bloom from summer into fall.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow flowers arranged in flat-topped clusters, each individual flower looking like a tiny button with no petals - just dense centers of disc flowers

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided, fern-like leaves that are strongly aromatic when crushed, releasing a pungent camphor-mint smell that can be almost overwhelming

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright stems 2-4 feet tall growing in patches or colonies, with a sturdy, somewhat woody base that persists through winter

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dry seeds with tiny ridges that form after the button flowers fade, often persisting into winter as brown clusters

habitat: Tansy thrives in disturbed soils along roadsides, old fields, pasture edges, and abandoned farmsteads throughout New England. It prefers sunny spots with well-drained soil and is often found near stone walls or old foundations where European settlers once cultivated it. You'll commonly see it growing alongside other non-native plants like Queen Anne's lace and chicory.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as rosettes of deeply cut leaves with that distinctive strong scent. Young plants are entirely leafy without flower stalks.
seasonality.summer: Tall flowering stems develop and bright yellow button flowers begin blooming in mid to late summer, attracting various small insects and beetles.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue blooming well into fall, eventually turning brown but often persisting on the plant. Seeds mature and disperse in late fall.
seasonality.winter: Dried brown flower clusters and sturdy stems remain standing above snow, making winter identification possible by the persistent button-like flower heads.

funFact: Tansy was once so valued as a natural insect repellent that colonial Americans packed it in their coffins to keep bugs away from the deceased - and they scattered tansy leaves on floors to repel fleas and ants from their homes.
confusionNotes: Tansy's button-like flowers might be confused with wild chamomile, but tansy's flowers are purely yellow buttons with no white petals, and tansy has that unmistakable strong camphor smell that chamomile lacks. Remember: if it smells like medicine and has only yellow buttons, it's tansy.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its innocent appearance, tansy contains compounds that can be toxic to livestock and humans in large quantities, which is why many states now consider it an invasive species. Early herbalists used tiny amounts medicinally, but modern foragers should admire its beauty and leave it alone.
compareHints: Tansy differs from its cousin feverfew by having purely yellow button flowers instead of feverfew's white daisy-like blooms with yellow centers. Dune tansy, found mainly on coastal areas, is much shorter and has more silvery foliage, while common tansy is taller with bright green leaves and grows inland.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its cousin tansy which has button-like yellow flowers with no white petals, feverfew always has the classic white daisy appearance.
Compared to common tansy, dune tansy is much shorter and more compact, adapted for harsh coastal conditions rather than inland meadows.
